deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler, §43, 'find all divisors of p^2+39q^2'. He combines Lagrange's reduction theory with his own residue-class method mod 4n = 156.

Step 1, reduced forms. Divisors D of p^2+39q^2 (with p, q coprime) are represented by forms f r^2 + 2g rs + h s^2 with fh = g^2 + 39, i.e. discriminant -156. Lagrange reduction (|2g| ≤ f ≤ h) gives 4g^2 ≤ fh = g^2 + n, so g ≤ sqrt(n/3) = sqrt(13) < 4. Hence g = 0, 1, 2, 3.
- g=0, fh=39: r^2+39s^2 (D=F) and 3r^2+13s^2 (3D=F).
- g=1, fh=40: r^2+2rs+40s^2 is equivalent to the principal form. 2r^2+2rs+20s^2 and 4r^2+2rs+10s^2 are imprimitive and are rightly discarded as giving no primes. 5r^2+2rs+8s^2 gives 5D=F (also 8D=F).
- g=2, fh=43 (prime): only the principal form again.
- g=3, fh=48: r^2+6rs+48s^2 is principal. 3r^2+6rs+16s^2 = 3(r+s)^2+13s^2 is equivalent to 3r^2+13s^2. The pairs (2,24), (4,12), (6,8) are imprimitive, so 'numeros primos continentes' silently excludes them.
Result: three 'genera' (really form classes up to orientation): D=F, 3D=F, 5D=F.

Step 2, residues. Euler lists the 24 residues below 78 coprime to 156 (φ(156)=48). He assigns signed residues ±a to the classes:
- Squares go to class I: 1, 25, 49, 11^2 ≡ -35, 17^2 ≡ -23, 19^2 ≡ 49, 23^2 ≡ 61.
- From 1+39 = 40, the prime 5 lies in class III. Multiplying the class-I residues by 5 and reducing gives class III: 5, 41, -31, -19, -67, -7.
- From p=2 he gets 43, in class I. From p=3 he gets 48, whose divisor 3 is excluded. From p=4 he gets 55 = 5·11, and continues with 11 on the next page.

Modern view. The primitive class group of discriminant -156 has order 4 and is cyclic. The classes are [1,0,39] (identity), [3,0,13] (order 2), and [5,±2,8] (order 4). There are only 2 genera:
- the principal genus {[1,0,39], [3,0,13]};
- the other genus {[5,±2,8]}.
So Euler's congruence method can only separate genera. That is why on the next page class II 'disappears' into class I. He then explains this by noting that 3t^2+13u^2 represents the square 16, so the classes coincide once denominators are allowed. For example, 61 = 3·4^2 + 13·1^2 = (25/4)^2 + 39(3/4)^2. In modern terms, forms in the same genus are rationally equivalent.
errors: The text has 'tria genera diuisorum: 1) D=F, 2) 3D=F, 5D=F'. The label '3)' is missing before 5D=F (likely a typesetting slip).
'19=+49' should read 19^2 = +49 (361 - 312 = 49). This is also in the printed text, as a misprint.
Conceptual gap. Euler counts the form 5r^2+2rs+8s^2 as a single 'genus', not distinguishing it from 5r^2-2rs+8s^2. He therefore misses that the class group has order 4 and is cyclic.

His later claim that 'no divisors of the second class remain' conflates class with genus. Primes such as 61 are genuinely represented by 3x^2+13y^2 and not by x^2+39y^2 in integers. Euler partly acknowledges this on the next page.
Imprimitive forms (2,6,24), (4,6,12), (6,6,8) for g=3 are skipped without comment. This is harmless.

ideas.what: Enumeration of reduced binary quadratic forms with fh = g^2+n and g ≤ sqrt(n/3), for n=39
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange–Gauss reduction; class enumeration for discriminant -156
ideas.where_published: Earlier in E598 itself, following Lagrange's Recherches d'arithmétique

ideas.what: Assigning residues a mod 4n to classes via squares, then multiplying by represented primes (5, 11, 43)
ideas.modern_name: Genus characters / quadratic reciprocity seen through residue classes mod 4n; multiplicativity of genera
ideas.where_published: E164 and related papers on divisors of pp±nqq (Comment. Acad. Petrop. XIV); E598

ideas.what: Using the identity-class/genus coincidence: a form that represents a square is identified with the principal form when rational values are allowed
ideas.modern_name: Forms in the same genus are rationally equivalent (genus = rational equivalence class)
ideas.where_published: E598 §44 (next page); similar fraction remarks in §41

missed.claim: Euler's procedure on this page is essentially a computation of genera: the residue method mod 156 can separate only the 2 genera, not the 4 classes. His subsequent explanation (a form representing a square merges with the principal class over Q) is an explicit pre-Gaussian example of 'same genus ⇔ rational equivalence'. This is probably noted in specialist histories (Weil, Edwards) only in general terms.
missed.quote: omnino dari tria genera diuisorum: 1) D=F, 2) 3D=F, 5D=F
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor historical point: a concrete 1770s instance of genus collapsing classes. It is of interest to historians of genus theory, not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example of Lagrange reduction plus Euler's residue method. The genus/class conflation it reveals is a known feature of Euler's approach. The rational-equivalence remark lives mostly on the next page and is mildly interesting, but likely known to historians.
transcription_corrections: The page heading reads '310'; the printed list '1) D=F, 2) 3D=F, 5D=F' lacks the '3)' label in the original as well.
'Q q 3 n =' at the bottom of the previous page is the signature mark 'Qq 3' followed by the catchword 'n ='.
